title: The Specimen Decides: Leprosy Signs, Ulcer Swabs and Clostridioides difficile Stools
summary: Three Chapter 59 calls that are settled before any stain: the clinical criteria and slit-skin smear that diagnose leprosy, why a surface swab of a decubitus ulcer cannot serve for anaerobic culture, and which stool a Clostridioides difficile algorithm may accept.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 59 Hit 12 (M. leprae cardinal signs; lepromatous vs tuberculoid bacillary load), Hit 15 (superficial decubitus-ulcer swabs for anaerobic culture) and Hit 16 (C. difficile GDH/toxin/NAAT algorithm). Checked against the IDSA/ASM laboratory utilization guide (Baron 2013), Chen 2022 on leprosy and Lee 2021 on C. difficile over-diagnosis, all read as Europe PMC full text. Three qualifications are flagged: the reviewer lists three cardinal signs but WHO pairs the lesion with definite sensory loss and makes a positive acid-fast smear the third sign; the reviewer calls superficial swabs simply “unacceptable”, while the guide treats a flocked swab in anaerobic transport as a second choice and surface cultures of decubitus ulcers specifically as not valuable; and the reviewer presents toxin-gene NAAT alone as an acceptable stand-alone, which current guidance limits to laboratories with preagreed stool-submission criteria. Not taught: leprosy treatment regimens, serology, reactions, anaerobic identification, C. difficile therapy.

objectives: State the clinical criteria and the smear findings on which a leprosy diagnosis rests, and how the tuberculoid and lepromatous poles differ in bacillary load.
Explain why a surface swab of a decubitus ulcer cannot support an anaerobic culture and which specimen replaces it.
Apply the preanalytic rules for Clostridioides difficile testing and state what GDH, NAAT and the toxin immunoassay each detect.

scenes.title: Three requests, one shift
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three requests reach the bench in one shift — (1) a traveller from a leprosy-endemic area with a pale, numb patch and a thickened ulnar nerve, request written as “culture for M. leprae”; (2) a cotton swab rubbed over the surface of a sacral decubitus ulcer, labelled “anaerobic culture”; (3) a formed stool labelled “Clostridioides difficile NAAT — test of cure”. Question token: “Which of these can the lab actually answer?”

cues.text: Three requests reach the bench in one shift. A traveller with a pale, numb skin patch and a thickened nerve at the elbow, with the request written as culture for Mycobacterium leprae.
A cotton swab rubbed over the surface of a sacral pressure ulcer, labelled anaerobic culture. And a formed stool labelled Clostridioides difficile test of cure.
Which of these can the laboratory actually answer?

props.label: Which can the lab actually answer?

scenes.title: What each diagnosis really rests on
scenes.altText: Schematic: three specimen pathways. Leprosy card — the WHO diagnostic criteria are a hypopigmented or reddish skin lesion with definite loss of sensation, a thickened or enlarged peripheral nerve with sensory loss or muscle weakness, and a positive acid-fast skin smear or bacilli in a smear or biopsy; diagnostic accuracy reaches about 95% when all three are present; M. leprae is an obligate intracellular bacillus with tropism for skin phagocytes and Schwann cells, and the main laboratory way to grow it is in mouse footpads. Anaerobes card — tissue, fluid, aspirate or biopsy in a sterile anaerobic container is the specimen of choice, with a flocked swab in an anaerobic transport device only as second choice; a Gram stain is requested with every anaerobic culture to judge specimen adequacy. C. difficile card — a diarrhoeal stool loose enough to take the shape of the container, from a patient with unexplained new-onset three or more unformed stools in 24 hours.

cues.text: Start with what each diagnosis rests on. Leprosy is a clinical diagnosis. The World Health Organization criteria are a pale or reddish skin lesion with definite loss of sensation, a thickened or enlarged peripheral nerve with sensory loss or muscle weakness, and bacilli demonstrated in a skin smear or biopsy.

With all three signs present, reported diagnostic accuracy reaches about ninety-five percent. Mycobacterium leprae is an obligate intracellular bacillus that targets skin phagocytes and Schwann cells, and the main way laboratories grow it is in mouse footpads, so no routine culture plate is waiting for it.

For anaerobes, the specimen of choice is tissue, fluid, an aspirate or a biopsy in a sterile anaerobic container. A flocked swab in an anaerobic transport device is only a second choice, and a Gram stain is requested with every anaerobic culture to judge whether the specimen is worth culturing.

For Clostridioides difficile, the specimen is a diarrhoeal stool, loose enough to take the shape of the container, from a patient with unexplained new-onset diarrhoea of three or more unformed stools in twenty-four hours.

props.title: C. difficile: diarrhoeal stool
lines: Takes the shape of the container

scenes.title: What the wrong specimen does
scenes.altText: Schematic: the wrong specimen produces a confident wrong answer. Swab card — three documented limitations of swabs versus tissue or aspirate: greater risk of contamination with surface or colonizing flora, limited quantity of specimen, and drying unless placed in transport medium, which itself dilutes out rare microbes. Ulcer card — surface cultures of wounds including decubitus ulcers are not valuable because they usually represent colonizing microbes that cannot be distinguished from the underlying etiologic agent; tissue biopsies after thorough debridement, or bone biopsy through a debrided site, are most valuable, and swab cultures of sinus tracts are not diagnostic. Stool card — formed stools should be rejected, with the proviso that a formed stool from a patient with ileus or possible toxic megacolon noted by the physician should be tested; repeat testing as a test of cure is not appropriate; retesting after a negative nucleic acid amplification test should not be done for at least six days, and one review advises avoiding retesting within seven days of a negative test.

cues.text: Now the damage. Swabs lose to tissue and aspirates for three documented reasons: a greater risk of picking up surface and colonizing flora, a limited quantity of material, and drying unless they sit in transport medium, which itself dilutes out the rare organisms you were hunting.

That is why surface cultures of wounds, decubitus ulcers included, are not valuable. They usually grow colonizing microbes that cannot be separated from the true cause. Tissue biopsy after thorough debridement, or bone biopsy through a debrided site, is the valuable specimen, and swabs of sinus tracts are not diagnostic.

On the stool side, a formed stool should be rejected, with one proviso: when the physician notes ileus or possible toxic megacolon, a formed stool is tested, because the patient may be unable to pass diarrhoea at all.

And repeat testing has rules. Retesting as a test of cure is not appropriate, and after a negative nucleic acid amplification test, retesting should wait at least six days, with one review advising no retesting within seven days.

props.label: No test of cure · wait ≥6 days

scenes.title: Reading what you get back
scenes.altText: Result reading. Leprosy card — slit-skin smear has about 100% specificity but only about 50% sensitivity; preferred sites are active lesions or lesions with altered sensitivity, plus ear lobes and the contralateral elbow; the bacterial index splits paucibacillary (under 2+) from multibacillary (2+ or more); at the tuberculoid pole patients have a strong cell-mediated response, few lesions, undetectable bacilli, granulomas on biopsy and a positive lepromin (Mitsuda) reaction, while at the lepromatous pole patients are anergic to M. leprae with multiple lesions and an infiltrate replete with bacilli; PCR sensitivity is about 87–100% with a positive bacterial index or lepromatous disease but about 30–83% with a negative index or tuberculoid disease. C. difficile card — GDH is a conserved enzyme present in every isolate, toxigenic or not; NAAT detects the toxin genes tcdA and tcdB and cannot separate carriage from active toxin production; the toxin A/B immunoassay shows active toxin but is the least sensitive, about 51–63%. Hook answers: diagnose leprosy clinically with a slit-skin smear or biopsy rather than a culture; reject the ulcer surface swab and ask for deep tissue after debridement in anaerobic transport; reject the formed stool sent as a test of cure.

cues.text: Now read what comes back. A slit-skin smear is close to one hundred percent specific but only about fifty percent sensitive, so a negative smear settles nothing. Sample active lesions or lesions with altered sensation, plus the ear lobes and the opposite elbow.

The bacterial index then sorts the case: below two plus is paucibacillary, two plus or more is multibacillary. At the tuberculoid pole, immunity is strong, lesions are few, bacilli are undetectable, biopsy shows granulomas and the lepromin reaction is positive. At the lepromatous pole, the patient is anergic to the bacillus, lesions are many and the infiltrate is replete with bacilli. PCR follows the same gradient: about eighty-seven to one hundred percent sensitive in multibacillary disease, but as low as thirty percent in tuberculoid disease.

On the stool side, remember what each test sees. GDH is an enzyme every isolate makes, toxin-producing or not. The amplification test finds the toxin genes, not the toxin, so it cannot separate a carrier from an infection. The toxin immunoassay shows active toxin but is the least sensitive, about fifty-one to sixty-three percent.

So the shift resolves: diagnose the leprosy case clinically with a smear or biopsy, not a culture; ask for deep tissue after debridement instead of the ulcer surface swab; and reject the formed stool sent as a test of cure.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A negative slit-skin smear rules out leprosy” (✓ sensitivity is only about 50%, and at the tuberculoid pole bacilli are undetectable); “A surface swab is fine as long as it goes in anaerobic transport” (✓ surface cultures of decubitus ulcers grow colonizers; tissue or aspirate after debridement is the valuable specimen); “Repeat the Clostridioides difficile test to prove cure” (✓ test of cure is not appropriate, and retesting after a negative amplification test waits at least six days).

cues.text: Trap one: a negative slit-skin smear rules out leprosy. No. The smear is about fifty percent sensitive, and at the tuberculoid pole bacilli are undetectable.

Trap two: a surface swab is fine as long as it travels in anaerobic transport. No. Surface cultures of a decubitus ulcer grow colonizers; the valuable specimen is tissue or an aspirate after debridement.
Trap three: repeat the Clostridioides difficile test to prove cure. No. Test of cure is not appropriate, and retesting after a negative amplification test waits at least six days.

props.title: ✗ “Surface swab is fine in anaerobic transport.”
lines: ✓ Colonizers; take tissue or aspirate after debridement

props.title: ✗ “Retest to prove cure.”
lines: ✓ No test of cure; wait ≥6 days after a negative NAAT

scenes.title: Deep, definite, diarrhoeal
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Three D’s for three requests — DEEP tissue for anaerobes, DEFINITE loss of sensation (plus nerve, plus smear) for leprosy, DIARRHOEAL stool for Clostridioides difficile.” Tokens: Deep = anaerobes · Definite = leprosy · Diarrhoeal = C. difficile. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: three D’s for three requests. Deep tissue for anaerobes. Definite loss of sensation, plus the thickened nerve and the smear, for leprosy. Diarrhoeal stool for Clostridioides difficile.

Where it breaks: a flocked swab in anaerobic transport is an accepted second choice when tissue cannot be obtained; a formed stool is tested when the physician notes ileus or possible toxic megacolon; and loss of sensation is not always present in leprosy, so biopsy or PCR may still be needed.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Leprosy: lesion with sensory loss + thickened nerve + bacilli in smear/biopsy”, “Anaerobes: deep tissue, not a surface swab · Clostridioides difficile: diarrhoeal stool, no test of cure”.

cues.text: Leprosy is diagnosed from a skin lesion with definite sensory loss, a thickened peripheral nerve and bacilli in a smear or biopsy rather than from a culture, anaerobic culture needs deep tissue or an aspirate rather than a surface swab of a pressure ulcer, and Clostridioides difficile testing needs a diarrhoeal stool and never a test of cure.

props.label: Leprosy: sensory loss + thickened nerve + bacilli
Deep tissue for anaerobes · diarrhoeal stool, no test of cure

explanation.what: Plain language: three very different requests fail for the same reason — the specimen cannot carry the answer. Leprosy is recognised from a numb skin lesion, a thickened nerve and bacilli seen in a smear, because the organism is not grown on routine plates. Anaerobes must come from deep tissue, because the skin surface is already full of harmless bacteria. And Clostridioides difficile testing only means something on a liquid stool from someone with new diarrhoea. Scientific terms: slit-skin smear, bacterial index (BI), paucibacillary and multibacillary disease, tuberculoid (TT) and lepromatous (LL) poles, lepromin (Mitsuda) reaction, anaerobic transport device, debridement, colonizing flora, glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH), toxin A/B enzyme immunoassay, nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT; tcdA/tcdB).
explanation.why: Each test has a population it was validated in. A slit-skin smear is near-perfectly specific but half-sensitive, so a negative smear cannot overrule the clinical signs. A surface swab samples colonizers that cannot be distinguished from the pathogen, so the culture report misleads treatment. A highly sensitive stool NAAT detects toxin genes in carriers, so testing people without diarrhoea — or retesting as a test of cure — converts carriage into a diagnosis.
explanation.measure: Leprosy: a hypopigmented or reddish lesion with definite loss of sensation, a thickened or enlarged peripheral nerve with sensory loss or weakness, and acid-fast bacilli in a skin smear or biopsy; about 95% diagnostic accuracy when all three are present; slit-skin smear specificity about 100%, sensitivity about 50%; bacterial index below 2+ paucibacillary, 2+ or more multibacillary; PCR sensitivity about 87–100% with a positive index or lepromatous disease versus about 30–83% with a negative index or tuberculoid disease. Anaerobic culture: tissue, fluid, aspirate or biopsy in a sterile anaerobic container, delivered at room temperature; flocked swab in an anaerobic transport device as second choice, room temperature, 2 h. Clostridioides difficile: diarrhoeal stool loose enough to take the shape of the container, from unexplained new-onset three or more unformed stools in 24 h; no test of cure; no retest for at least 6 days after a negative NAAT; sensitivity roughly 92–97% for NAAT, 86–99% for GDH, 51–63% for toxin A/B immunoassay, over 95% for toxigenic culture.
explanation.differs: Tuberculoid pole (strong cell-mediated response, granulomas, undetectable bacilli, positive lepromin) versus lepromatous pole (anergic, multiple lesions, infiltrate replete with bacilli); surface swab (colonizers, little material, drying) versus tissue or aspirate after debridement; GDH (every isolate) versus NAAT (toxin genes) versus toxin immunoassay (active toxin).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: name the specimen that is unacceptable for anaerobic culture and its replacement, decide whether a formed stool or a repeat Clostridioides difficile request should be run, or match a leprosy case to the tuberculoid or lepromatous pole by lesion count and bacillary load.

mnemonic.text: Three D’s for three requests: DEEP tissue for anaerobes, DEFINITE loss of sensation (plus the thickened nerve and the smear) for leprosy, DIARRHOEAL stool for Clostridioides difficile.
mnemonic.explanation: Ties each request to the one specimen or sign that can carry its answer.
mnemonic.limitation: The three D’s hide the exceptions: a flocked swab in an anaerobic transport device is an accepted second choice when tissue or aspirate cannot be obtained, a formed stool is tested when the physician notes ileus or possible toxic megacolon, and definite loss of sensation is not always present in leprosy, so biopsy or PCR may still be needed.

analogyLimitations: The three requests are an invented scenario.
Specimens, ulcer and organisms are drawn as schematic cards, not images.
Sensitivity and specificity figures are review and guideline summaries; kits, readers and sampling sites differ.
takeaway: Leprosy is diagnosed from a skin lesion with definite sensory loss, a thickened peripheral nerve and bacilli in a smear or biopsy rather than from a culture, anaerobic culture needs deep tissue or an aspirate rather than a surface swab of a pressure ulcer, and Clostridioides difficile testing needs a diarrhoeal stool and never a test of cure

questions.stem: A superficial swab taken from the surface of a sacral decubitus ulcer is submitted for anaerobic culture. What should the laboratory do, and why?

options.text: Ask for tissue or an aspirate from the debrided wound in an anaerobic container, because a surface culture grows colonizing flora that cannot be distinguished from the true pathogen
options.rationale: Correct. Surface cultures of wounds including decubitus ulcers are not valuable; tissue biopsy after thorough debridement is the valuable specimen.

options.text: Culture the swab and report every isolate with susceptibilities
options.rationale: Incorrect. The isolates would largely be surface colonizers, and reporting them as pathogens misdirects therapy.

options.text: Culture the swab but add a 30°C set
options.rationale: Incorrect. A second temperature addresses cutaneous mycobacteria, not the contamination problem of a surface swab.

options.text: Refrigerate the swab and hold it until a deep specimen arrives
options.rationale: Incorrect. Holding and chilling the wrong specimen does not fix it; anaerobic specimens travel at room temperature and the deep specimen should be requested now.

questions.stem: A man from a leprosy-endemic area has a hypopigmented patch with definite loss of sensation and a thickened ulnar nerve. The slit-skin smear shows no acid-fast bacilli. Which interpretation is best supported?

options.text: The findings still fit leprosy; the smear is highly specific but only about 50% sensitive, and bacilli are undetectable at the tuberculoid pole
options.rationale: Correct. A negative smear cannot overrule the clinical criteria, and tuberculoid disease is paucibacillary.

options.text: Leprosy is excluded because the smear is negative
options.rationale: Incorrect. Smear sensitivity is only about 50%, so a negative result does not exclude the diagnosis.

options.text: A routine culture on Löwenstein–Jensen medium should settle it
options.rationale: Incorrect. M. leprae is an obligate intracellular bacillus; the main laboratory means of growing it is mouse footpad inoculation, not routine culture.

options.text: The negative smear means the disease must be lepromatous
options.rationale: Incorrect. The lepromatous pole is the bacilli-rich end of the spectrum, where smears are strongly positive.

questions.stem: Which Clostridioides difficile request should the laboratory decline?

options.text: A repeat test after successful treatment, requested as a test of cure
options.rationale: Correct. Repeat testing as a test of cure is not appropriate, and retesting after a negative NAAT should wait at least 6 days.

options.text: A diarrhoeal stool from an inpatient with unexplained new-onset ≥3 unformed stools in 24 hours
options.rationale: Incorrect. This is the target population for testing.

options.text: A formed stool from a patient whose physician notes ileus with possible toxic megacolon
options.rationale: Incorrect. This is the stated exception in which a formed stool is tested.

options.text: A loose stool that takes the shape of its container from a patient with new watery diarrhoea
options.rationale: Incorrect. That consistency is exactly what the diarrhoeal-stool requirement describes.

claims.text: WHO leprosy diagnostic criteria, their combined accuracy, and that sensory loss may be absent.
Slit-skin smear specificity about 100% and sensitivity about 50%; sampling sites; bacterial index thresholds; PCR sensitivity by pole.
Tuberculoid pole paucibacillary with granulomas and positive lepromin; lepromatous pole anergic with an infiltrate replete with bacilli.
M. leprae is an obligate intracellular bacillus targeting skin phagocytes and Schwann cells, grown in laboratories in mouse footpads.

Swab limitations versus tissue or aspirate; surface cultures of wounds including decubitus ulcers are not valuable; biopsy after debridement is most valuable; sinus-tract swabs are not diagnostic; anaerobic specimen of choice and transport.
Diarrhoeal stool required; formed stool rejected unless ileus or possible toxic megacolon is noted; no test of cure; no retest for at least 6 days after a negative NAAT (one review advises 7 days).
What GDH, NAAT and the toxin A/B immunoassay detect, with their sensitivity ranges, and when NAAT alone is acceptable.
Whether M. leprae is strictly non-cultivable on any artificial medium (the reviewer-style claim that it cannot be cultured at all).
claims.note: No open source read in this session states this outright; the lesson teaches only that M. leprae is an obligate intracellular bacillus grown in mouse footpads, as Chen 2022 states.

claims.text: The three-request shift is invented; cards are schematic.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 59 Hit 12 gives the cardinal signs as “skin lesions + cutaneous anesthesia + enlarged peripheral nerves”. The WHO criteria as reported by Chen 2022 pair the lesion WITH definite loss of sensation, require sensory loss or muscle weakness with the thickened nerve, and make a positive acid-fast skin smear or bacilli in a smear/biopsy the third sign; the same review notes that loss of sensation is not always present. The lesson teaches the WHO wording (register flag rv-leprosy-cardinal-signs-smear).

Ch. 59 Hit 15 calls superficial swabs of decubitus ulcers simply “unacceptable for anaerobic culture”. Baron 2013 states that surface cultures of such wounds are not valuable because they represent colonizers, but also lists a flocked swab in an anaerobic swab transport device as an acceptable second choice when tissue, fluid or an aspirate cannot be obtained. The lesson teaches both halves (register flag rv-decubitus-swab-second-choice).

Ch. 59 Hit 16 presents “toxin-gene NAAT” as an acceptable stand-alone alternative to the GDH-plus-toxin algorithm. Lee 2021, summarising the 2017 IDSA/SHEA guidance, limits NAAT alone to laboratories with preagreed stool-submission criteria and otherwise recommends a toxin test within a multistep algorithm; the hit also omits the preanalytic rules (diarrhoeal stool only, no test of cure, no early retest) that Baron 2013 gives. The lesson teaches the preanalytic rules and the conditional status of NAAT alone (register flag rv-cdiff-naat-alone-criteria).

The specimen-acceptability and Clostridioides difficile testing rules taught here come from US professional guidance (IDSA/ASM 2013 and the IDSA/SHEA recommendations as summarised by Lee 2021). Philippine regulatory requirements and local laboratory rules are not covered and may differ.

morphology.note: No micrographs or clinical photographs; specimens, lesions and tests are shown as schematic cards.

verification.notes: Seven factual claims checked against Baron 2013 (IDSA/ASM utilization guide), Chen 2022 and Lee 2021, all read as Europe PMC full text; 1 pending (whether M. leprae is strictly non-cultivable), which is not taught. The 2017 IDSA/SHEA C. difficile guideline itself had no full text in Europe PMC and was not read directly; its recommendations are taught only as Lee 2021 reports them. No human expert has reviewed this lesson.
